extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Mill's principles and criteria about induction, the limits of tests like 'inconceivability', and distinctions between genuine induction and other reasoning forms for evaluating scientific and everyday inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the inconceivability test (Spencer’s test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test that a proposition is true because its negation is inconceivable is only legitimately applicable to propositions which are assented to on simple inspection, without any intervening media of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill grants the limitation but argues it still fails for many famously false or groundless beliefs once classed as complex; consciousness often gives no verdict for complex propositions until media of proof are supplied. Examples/antipatterns: treating complex scientific truths as if their negation were inconceivable (e.g., early intuitions about sunrise/sunset or gravitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between simple and complex propositions for testing truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple propositions (subject and predicate in direct relation) may be amenable to immediate consciousness tests; complex propositions (indirectly related through many simple propositions) are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply immediate-inspection criteria to propositions that require mediating proofs (e.g., geometric theorems). Beware of false confidence when a proposition appears simple but rests on unexamined mediating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconclusiveness of inconceivability as evidence of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivability is not a reliable criterion of impossibility or of necessary truth; inability to imagine a fact's possibility does not justify inferring its impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill (and Sir William Hamilton) argue that some truths may be true though our understanding cannot construe their possibility; conversely, what seems inconceivable may still be false. Example: after learning Copernican proof, one can still imagine sunset as sun-moving though one believes otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is the appropriate test of empirical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: To test an empirical proposition, appeal to experience: recurring observation, lack of counter-instances, and broad agreement among observers constitute the proper evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill rejects interpreting 'appeal to experience' as mentally checking every single instance; it suffices that one has repeatedly observed the fact and others with opportunities concur. Beware of substituting mere familiarity for sufficiency of evidence; the inconceivability-test measures familiarity, not probative sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited or innate convictions need independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if mental tendencies are inherited and thus seem a priori in the individual, this does not guarantee the truth of the corresponding beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherited tendencies may reflect ancestral error rather than objective truth; therefore such convictions should be subjected to empirical or rational scrutiny rather than taken as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Contradiction understood empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: The Principle of Contradiction (that the same proposition cannot be both true and false) can be regarded as a generalization from experience—that belief and disbelief are distinct mental states excluding each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill prefers treating it as an empirical generalization rather than a mere verbal identity; justify the axiom by simple introspection of mental states and external contrasts (light/darkness etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope of the Principle of Excluded Middle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Principle of Excluded Middle (either a proposition or its negation must be true) holds only when the predicate can intelligibly be attributed to the subject; otherwise a third possibility—'unmeaning'—exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend excluded middle to statements about noumena or predicates that lack intelligible sense (e.g., 'Abracadabra is a second intention'). The axiom requires qualification: the predicate must be meaningfully predicable of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the operation of discovering and proving general propositions; more broadly, it is the process by which inference from known to unknown (including single facts) is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inductions to individuals and to generals as the same logical operation: whenever evidence from observed cases justifies inferring about unobserved similar cases, induction is at work. This makes the logic of science applicable to practical reasoning and common life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine induction vs mere abridgement ('perfect induction')
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine induction proceeds from known to unknown (infers beyond premises); a so-called 'perfect' induction that simply abbreviates a list of already-known instances (e.g., 'all known planets') is not genuine induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count mere summation of observed instances as induction. A true general proposition asserts more than the sum of its premises (it claims applicability to unknown or future instances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality implies unlimited scope (past, present, and future)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition (e.g., 'All men are mortal') intends to apply to all individuals of the class—past, present, and future—not merely those observed or counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a claim is truly general, check whether it is being asserted as universal (extends to unobserved cases) rather than as an enumeration of known individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of instances depends on number and nature, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify a generalization, it is the number and character (representativeness, relevance) of observed instances that matter, not that every existing instance has been examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the mistaken requirement to observe every individual; instead assess whether the sampled instances are enough in kind and variety to support inference. Example: inferring 'all animals have nervous systems' may be legitimate without checking every species if instances sampled are suitably varied and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is distinct from mathematical/demonstrative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical demonstrations and parity-of-reasoning (showing a property for representative figures or using a priori grounds) are not inductions because they rely on demonstrative evidence rather than inference from particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposition is shown via demonstration (e.g., geometric proof or a priori combinatorial argument), it is not properly an inductive conclusion, even if it has universal form. Beware of labeling mathematical pattern-spotting as induction without recognizing underlying a priori justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between induction and descriptive synthesis of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining a sequence of partial observations into a single descriptive representation (e.g., calling a circumnavigated land an 'island' or expressing planetary observations as an ellipse) is often a summary of observed facts, not an induction inferring beyond them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the conclusion asserts anything beyond the observed parts. If the 'general conception' merely summarizes what was observed, it is not an inductive inference; if it posits unobserved features based on observed pattern, it may be inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires specifying assignable respects of resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: An inductive inference asserts that what is true of certain individuals will be true of all cases which resemble them in certain assignable respects; those respects must be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful induction depends on articulating the relevant similarities that justify projecting predicates to unobserved cases. Vague or unassignable resemblance undermines legitimacy of the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of selection in practical inference (advocacy/judicial contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical or forensic inquiry the chief difficulty is not testing inductions but selecting which known general propositions to apply to a particular case; skill lies in fitting the case under appropriate general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practitioners, cultivate knowledge of relevant general principles and sagacity in mapping a specific case onto those principles. Once selected, the validity of the application is tested by the same logical rules as in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of experiment and theory enhances inductive discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining inductive (experimental/observational) and deductive (theoretical) methods—each verifying the other's conclusions—forms a more powerful engine of discovery than either alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage the iterative use of experiment to test theory and theory to guide experiment; recognize that many scientific advances arise from this combined approach (Herschel’s observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as the source of non-intuitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: All knowledge that is not intuitive depends on induction; therefore, understanding what induction is and what conditions make it legitimate is central to logic and the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of non-self-evident truths, treat them as inductive in nature and subject them to the rules and tests of induction laid out (representativeness of instances, assignable resemblance, etc.).
